searches.note: Twenty six searches of a share of twenty eight, two left unspent, none of them the author's. One was shared across the group: the Wine of Origin seal and the vintage rule of 85 per cent. Six were restricted to a house's own domain (Kanonkop's pages, Meerlust's, Rustenberg's history and its sheets, Simonsig's sheets and its family history, Lanzerac's product pages); the first search for each house kept its domain out, so that each second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail stood in no source read, it was cut or said with less; the house's own claims stay told as its account. A claim of a first that a source disputes is now told as the claimant's count.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, a Master of Wine's blog, a writer's sparkling wine site) are cited neither in the fragment nor here. A winemag column whose address names a living writer is not cited.

The serving temperatures follow the Codex's service reference: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius for the three Bordeaux blends, 15 to 17 for the Pinotage, 8 to 10 for the Cap Classique; no air is promised to soften tannin. Sound on all five.

tested: Paul Sauer the man: 1898 to 1976, son of the minister J. W. Sauer, Minister of Railways from 1948 and of Lands from 1954, out of active politics by about 1963 (Wikipedia, South African History Online). The story's from 1948 into the 1960s stands. Sound.

The farm: Sauer bought it in 1919 and named it Kanonkop by the house; Club Oenologique says 1929 and that his father farmed Uitkyk above it. Founded stays empty, the story says after the First World War. Sound.

The first bottling of 1973, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage, pressed for by the son-in-law with the winemaker of the day: Club Oenologique and the house. Sound. The bulk sale to the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery for decades before: Club Oenologique; the unease is tied to it.
Sauer's death in January 1976 and the farm passing to his daughter (Club Oenologique, Wikipedia). Changed: the daughter, not the couple.
Paul Sauer the wine: first made in 1981 (the library, most accounts; one says first released in 1981); introduced by the winemaker who followed the first. Sound.

The making: open top concrete fermenters, the cap punched down by hand every two hours, 24 months in new 225 litre Nevers barrels (merchants' copies of the house's 2022 and 2023 notes, Findlater and Co and Cape Ardor among them). Sound.

The grapes: 2017 at 76 Cabernet Sauvignon, 17 Cabernet Franc, 7 Merlot; 2016 at 62 Cabernet Sauvignon, 25 Merlot, 13 Cabernet Franc (release notes found in one search with Club Oenologique's review of twelve vintages and merchants' pages; a Master of Wine's own site among them is not cited). Changed: the equal parts were wrong.

The cannon: the house says the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and a signal to farmers to take produce to the ships; Club Oenologique says the eighteenth and nineteenth. Kept as the house's account; left open.

The soils: decomposed or weathered granite on the house's pages; Hutton and Clovelly in no source, after a search on those words. Changed. The house's twenty to twenty five years: in no source. Changed.

Label, cards and questions: the ward, the Wine of Origin seal on the neck with its own number (SAWIS, Wine Spectator), one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach. Rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: Cabernet Sauvignon, traditionally about seven tenths, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot in roughly equal parts for the rest; the shares move with the year.
changed.now: Cabernet Sauvignon, from about three fifths to three quarters by year, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot for the rest in shares that also move with the year.
changed.why: The sheets read give Cabernet Sauvignon at 76 and 62 per cent in two neighbouring years, and Merlot well above Cabernet Franc in one and well below it in the other, so equal parts is wrong and seven tenths is only a middle.

changed.was: The name, as the house tells it, comes from a hillock on the Simonsberg above the farm, where in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a cannon was fired to announce sailing ships entering Table Bay. After the First World War the farm passed to Paul Sauer (1898 to 1976), son of a Cape cabinet minister and himself a minister in the National Party governments from 1948 into the 1960s. In 1973 his son-in-law and the estate's winemaker bottled the first wines under the Kanonkop label, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage among them; Sauer, by the house's account, was uneasy at first, for he had close ties to the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery. He died in 1976, and the farm passed to his daughter and her husband, the Krige family. With the 1981 vintage the estate made its first Bordeaux blend and gave it his name: Paul Sauer, Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc and Merlot, fermented in open concrete tanks with the cap punched down by hand and aged in new French oak. Kanonkop is known above all for Pinotage, yet Paul Sauer holds none, so it is no Cape Blend. For a sommelier it is the Stellenbosch Cabernet blend to name first, and the proof that Kanonkop is more than its Pinotage.

changed.was: Each variety is fermented apart, with pump overs and délestage, and goes through malolactic fermentation in barrel. After some months the components are blended and returned to French oak, mostly Nevers and more than half of it new, for sixteen to twenty one months in all; the wine then rests in bottle before release.
changed.now: Each parcel of each variety is fermented apart, with pump overs and délestage, and goes through malolactic fermentation in 300 litre French oak barrels, mostly Nevers and more than half new in the vintages whose sheets give a share. After about eight months the components are blended and returned to barrel, for sixteen to twenty one months in all; the wine then rests in bottle before release.
changed.why: Every parcel of each variety is fermented apart and goes through malolactic in 300 litre barrels; the components are blended after about eight months and go back to barrel for about ten more; 2016 spent 16 months in all and 2009 21; new oak is 55 to 70 per cent where a sheet gives it, mostly Nevers.

changed.was: A German settler took up the farm in 1693, as the estate tells it, and named it Meerlust, roughly the pleasure of the sea, for the view from its granite outcrop five kilometres from False Bay. In 1756 the Myburgh family bought it, eight generations by their own count. The homestead's front gable marks 1776, the year its extension was completed, and the whole farmstead has been declared a national monument. For more than two centuries Meerlust sold its grapes and wine in bulk; the seventh generation of the family turned it towards bottling under the estate's own name, beginning with a Cabernet Sauvignon in the 1970s. Drawn to Bordeaux, he and his winemaker set out to blend Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the Médoc manner, and the 1980 vintage became Rubicon, among the first Bordeaux blends of the modern Cape. A poet friend at the University of Stellenbosch suggested the name, as the family tells it: like crossing the Rubicon, the decision could not be undone. At his death in 1988 his son, the eighth generation, took over. For a sommelier Rubicon is where the Cape's Bordeaux blend begins, and a wine made to be kept.

changed.was: The farm goes back to 1682, when, as the estate tells it, a German settler from near the Rhine was granted the land. In 1810 an owner divided it into two farms, Rustenberg and Schoongezicht. Phylloxera struck the Cape's vineyards in the late nineteenth century, and in 1892 John X Merriman (1841 to 1926), the English born politician who would be the last prime minister of the Cape Colony, from 1908 to 1910, took on Schoongezicht, while his brother-in-law took Rustenberg; together they replanted on resistant rootstock. Wine has been bottled at the estate without a break since 1892, by its own account. In 1941 a member of the Barlow family, on leave from his army unit in the Second World War, bought Rustenberg, and in 1945 he added Schoongezicht, joining the two farms again after more than a century apart. The estate's Bordeaux blend carries Merriman's name and draws only on its own vineyards; beside it the single vineyard Peter Barlow Cabernet honours the buyer of 1941. For a sommelier, John X Merriman ties a Simonsberg red to a Cape prime minister, and to an estate that has bottled its own wine for well over a century.

changed.was: Simonsig's founder began to farm in 1953, as the family tells it, on De Hoop, a farm he rented from his father-in-law, and in 1964 he bought land of his own. In 1968 he bottled the first wine under the Simonsig name, a Chenin Blanc labelled Steen. A visit to Champagne led him to try its method at home: from the 1971 harvest, with rudimentary equipment and riddling racks he built himself, he made a sparkling wine fermented a second time in its bottle. The Cape grew little Chardonnay or Pinot Noir then, so the wine was Chenin Blanc. He called it Kaapse Vonkel, Cape sparkle, and released it in 1973, the first South African wine of its kind. In 1971, too, by the house's account, Simonsig joined Spier and Delheim in founding the Stellenbosch Wine Route. The blend later moved to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with a little Pinot Meunier beside them. As other cellars took up the method, the Cape's makers formed an association in 1992 and gave the style the name Méthode Cap Classique. For a sommelier, Kaapse Vonkel is where Cap Classique begins: the Cape's own name for the traditional method, and the bottle that started it.
changed.now: Simonsig's founder began to farm in 1953, as the family tells it, on De Hoop, a farm he rented from his father-in-law, and in the early 1960s he bought land of his own. In 1968 he bottled the first wine under the Simonsig name, a Chenin Blanc labelled Steen. Drawn to the method of Champagne, he made from the 1971 harvest a sparkling wine fermented a second time in its bottle. The Cape grew little Chardonnay or Pinot Noir then, so the wine was Chenin Blanc. He called it Kaapse Vonkel, Cape sparkle, and released it in 1973. Earlier Cape cellars had tried the method, but the Cap Classique producers count Kaapse Vonkel as the first wine of their category. In 1971, too, Simonsig was among the estates that founded the Stellenbosch Wine Route. In 1987 the blend moved to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and Pinot Meunier later joined them. As other cellars took up the method, the style took the name Méthode Cap Classique, and in 1992 its makers formed an association. For a sommelier, Kaapse Vonkel is where Cap Classique begins: the Cape's own name for the traditional method, and the bottle from which the category counts its years.
changed.why: The visit and the racks were in no source; the purchase year differs in the house's own pages; the first claim is contested; the 1987 move has two sources; the Wine Route had more than three founders by one account; the name and the association are told in the order the sources allow.

changed.was: Lanzerac dates itself to 1692, when, as the estate tells it, a settler took the land, named the farm Schoongezicht and planted its first vines. In 1920 a new owner bought the farm and renamed it Lanzerac; the story goes that the name honours a French general of the First World War, a tale told rather than recorded. In 1925, at the university in Stellenbosch, Abraham Perold (1880 to 1941), its first professor of viticulture, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, then called Hermitage, and gave the Cape its own grape. The first wine sold as Pinotage came from the 1959 vintage, from grapes grown and made at the Bellevue farm, by most accounts. It was judged the champion of the young wine show that year, and the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released it in 1961 under its Lanzerac label, as the Pinotage Association tells it. The estate counts that label as its own heritage, and its Lanzerac Pinotage, from its own Jonkershoek vineyards, carries the name forward. For a sommelier the lesson is in the detail: the first Pinotage label said Lanzerac, but by most accounts the grapes grew at Bellevue.

swaps.proposed: The author proposed replacing Lanzerac with Vergelegen (its V or GVB Red) or Warwick (Trilogy), since the first Pinotage of 1959 was grown and made at Bellevue and released by the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery under its Lanzerac label, so the plan's why overstates the estate's part, and Lanzerac is known as a hotel.
swaps.why: The record as written tells the history truly and hedges it: the 1961 label was the merchant's Lanzerac brand, a trademark it had bought from the estate in the late 1950s by one account, on Bellevue's wine by most accounts, and the estate marks the anniversary itself (its 60 years of Pinotage, its 1959 Commemoration Pinotage). A guest knows the name, and the label of 1961 is a fact the Codex already teaches (the Pinotage card: the name first appeared on a label in 1961). Both proposed wines are Bordeaux blends: with Paul Sauer, Rubicon and John X Merriman already in the group, a swap would leave four Bordeaux blends and no Pinotage flagship in the district where Pinotage was bred, and the region summary names Pinotage as the second of its three lessons. A new house now would also need a new record written and refuted from a spent allowance. What is wrong is the plan's why, not the pick.
swaps.planWhy: Jonkershoek estate whose name was on the 1961 label of the first wine sold as Pinotage, the 1959 vintage.
swaps.forReadTogether: Keep the pick and its key; change only the why in plan.json to the line above. No record edit is needed for the swap.
